title: Data Interpretation
relevance: SDE OAs and placement aptitude rounds use DI exhibits as a speed filter: extract the right numbers, approximate, and apply percentage/share/ratio without heavy arithmetic.

phases.goal: Establish that DI is a reading-and-extraction skill with light arithmetic and a fixed drill before calculating.

must_hit.point: Start every exhibit by reading the title, units, and legend first — half of all DI errors are unit slips (thousands vs lakhs, % vs absolute).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate names title/units/legend as the first step and cites unit slips as the common failure mode.

must_hit.point: The three workhorse operations are percentage change ((new−old)/old)×100, share (part/total)×100, and ratio.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate states all three formulas with the correct base for percentage change.

must_hit.point: For “which is largest / roughly what %” questions, approximate by rounding and comparing rather than computing to the last decimal.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate says exact figures are rarely needed for ranking or rough-percentage items and describes rounding before comparing.

must_hit.point: Compute a shared row or column total once and reuse it across sub-questions on the same exhibit.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate explains computing the total once and applying it to later questions instead of re-adding.

probes: Walk me through your first 10 seconds looking at a new DI table or chart before you touch any option.
What three calculations should you have cold for almost every DI set?

hints.1: Think about what goes wrong most often before any arithmetic starts.
hints.2: Name the pre-read checklist, then the three formulas, then when to approximate vs total once.
hints.3: Title/units/legend first (half of errors are unit slips); % change, share, ratio; approximate for largest/rough %; reuse one row/column total.

phases.goal: Show how to pull answers from tables, bars, pies, lines, and prose caselets using the right lookup or conversion.

must_hit.point: On a table, many questions are answered by reading a printed column or row total directly rather than summing from scratch.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate points to using the given year or product total when it is already in the table.

must_hit.point: Percentage change is always (new−old)/old×100 against the earlier base; a fall uses the same form with the earlier value in the denominator.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate writes (new−old)/old×100 and refuses to put the later value in the denominator.

must_hit.point: On a pie chart, a sector’s central angle is its percentage of a full circle of 360°.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate maps share% × 360° (e.g. 25% → 90°) without inventing another scale.

must_hit.point: In a caselet, convert each nested percentage into absolute headcount (or amount) first, then add or take the final ratio — never chain “percentage of a percentage” in your head.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate converts men/women and subgroup % to counts, then sums or forms the fraction from those counts.

probes: How do you find a year total or a product’s three-year total from a sales table?
A pie says Food is 25% of the budget — how do you get the central angle?
Office of 300 with 60% male; 25% of men and 40% of women in Sales — how do you get total Sales headcount?

hints.1: Decide whether the answer is already printed, needs a % formula, a pie angle, or absolute conversion.
hints.2: Table → read/reuse totals; change → divide by earlier base; pie → % of 360°; caselet → absolutes then combine.
hints.3: Read column/row totals when present; (new−old)/old×100; angle = share×360°; men/women counts then Sales counts before summing or taking Sales fraction.

phases.goal: Distinguish when to approximate vs compute exactly, and percentage vs absolute growth, under OA vs case-interview scoring.

must_hit.point: “Highest growth” almost always means highest percentage growth, not the largest absolute jump — the same absolute rise can yield different % rises when bases differ.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate compares % rises year-to-year and notes identical absolute +30 rises can differ in % because bases differ.

must_hit.point: When a question says “approximately,” round aggressively before dividing so you can eliminate wrong options without long division.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate describes rounding numerator/denominator first to get a nearby simple fraction and match the closest option.

must_hit.point: In an OA, graders see only the answer so ruthless approximation and one exact shared total win; in a case interview, say assumptions and the base you divide by out loud because reasoning is scored.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate contrasts OA speed/answer-only with case-interview need to narrate base and assumptions.

probes: Two years both rose by the same absolute amount — how do you decide which had higher growth?
How does your approach change between a timed OA DI set and a spoken case-interview DI question?

hints.1: Ask whether the stem wants percent or absolute, and who is scoring your work.
hints.2: Compare % with the earlier base; approximate when the stem says so; OA vs case changes what you optimize.
hints.3: Highest growth → % not absolute jump; approximate before dividing on “approximately”; OA = speed + shared totals, case = say base/assumptions aloud.

phases.goal: Apply DI drill and formulas to multi-question exhibits and OA-style target-growth projections under time pressure.

must_hit.point: DI in an OA is a speed filter: typically 4–6 questions on one exhibit in a couple of minutes, won by approximation and computing each shared total exactly once.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate cites the 4–6 questions / couple-of-minutes pattern and the reuse-of-totals tactic.

must_hit.point: Required growth to a future target is (target−current)/current×100 against the latest actual base — not the gap divided by an arbitrary number.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate divides the gap by the current-year base (e.g. growth needed to a stated target from last year’s revenue).

must_hit.point: On dual line series, “first overtake” means the first month the trailing series exceeds the leader; combined peak means summing both series per period and picking the max.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Candidate compares series month-by-month for crossover and adds both for the combined high.

probes: A company earned 210 last year and targets 250 next year — how do you find the approximate % growth needed?
On a two-product line chart, how do you find when B first overtakes A and which month has the highest combined sales?

hints.1: Name the base for target growth and what “overtake” vs “combined” each require.
hints.2: Target growth = gap over current base; overtake = first period B > A; combined = A+B per period.
hints.3: (250−210)/210×100 ≈ 19%; scan months until B exceeds A; sum A+B each month and take the peak.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: “Highest growth” almost always means percentage growth. Identical absolute rises (e.g. +30) can rank differently in % because each divides by a different earlier base — always check which the stem asks for.
When the stem says “approximately,” round before dividing to eliminate options fast; still compute a shared row/column total exactly once when many sub-questions reuse it.

OA is answer-only under a couple of minutes for 4–6 questions on one exhibit — optimize for ruthless approximation and one shared total. Case interviews score reasoning, so state assumptions and the base you divide by out loud.

gotchas.trap: Carrying a running “percentage of a percentage” in your head for nested groups.
gotchas.correction: Convert each percentage to absolute values first, then take the final sum or ratio.

gotchas.trap: Measuring percentage change against the later value instead of the earlier base.
gotchas.correction: Percentage change is always (new−old)/old against the earlier value — including for falls.

gotchas.trap: Treating “highest growth” as the largest absolute jump.
gotchas.correction: Compare year-on-year percentage rises; same absolute rise can mean different % when bases differ.

gotchas.trap: On a target-growth question, dividing the revenue gap by 100 or by some wrong prior year instead of by the current base.
gotchas.correction: Required % = (target−current)/current×100 using the latest actual revenue as the denominator.
